overview.text: The U.S. Department of the Interior (DOI) is a Cabinet-level executive department created by Congress on March 3, 1849, to bring together federal offices handling the nation’s internal affairs. Today, it protects and manages natural resources and cultural heritage, provides scientific information, and honors federal trust commitments to Indigenous peoples and communities. Its distinguishing feature is its wide reach: specialized bureaus work on public lands, national parks, wildlife, geology, water, and Indian affairs, so DOI is not simply a parks agency. Its history also reflects changing federal policy: Indian Affairs moved into Interior in 1849, while the department now describes its work with tribes in terms that include self-determination and self-governance.

key_facts.text: Congress created the department on March 3, 1849, consolidating several offices, including the General Land Office, Indian Affairs Office, and patent and pension offices.
DOI’s stated mission includes managing natural resources and cultural heritage, providing scientific information, and honoring trust responsibilities or special commitments to Indigenous communities.

Its bureaus have distinct roles: for example, the National Park Service manages park sites, the Bureau of Land Management manages public lands, and the U.S. Geological Survey provides science about natural resources and hazards.
The Bureau of Indian Affairs was established within the War Department in 1824 and transferred to Interior in 1849; the name “Bureau of Indian Affairs” was formally adopted in 1947.
The Bureau of Indian Affairs fulfills trust responsibilities and promotes self-determination and self-governance for federally recognized tribes and Alaska Natives.
